author: ohtadmin
title: Locals showcase talent at open mic night
text:
Now in the wake of its sixth edition, the Narragansett Cafe has been showcasing Jamestown’s talent with an open-mic night every third Wednesday of the month.
The cafe, locally known as The Ganny, has served as the backdrop for music, storytelling and laughter during its “Wednesday Night Live” events.
Jay Primiano, who has a podcast, “Catunquit Chronicles,” in addition to serving as an emcee for some of these evenings, describes the events as a performance showcase and community creative space.
“In the wintertime, people are looking for something to do,” he said. “The midweek gets a little troublesome. When the temperatures are as they are, it’s hard to get out. So, it’s nice for something to look forward to each month.”
Primiano also participates during the open mics, often singing songs, sharing his writings or performing improv. He shares emcee duties with Jan Greene, who, during the January edition, read an amusing poem about age that got plenty of laughs from the audience. She took up theater and improv in the last two years.
“I’m heading toward 78 and I’m doing things I wanted to do all my life,” she said.
Jane Gilgun, the artistic director of the program, rounds out the triumvirate of organizers. She was inspired to mimic the open-mic events she has witnessed at Irish pubs, describing them as “community building and lifting spirits. They were times of joy.”
“I like seeing people inviting people to get up on the stage and share their talents, share their perspective on things,” she said.
Primiano, Greene and Gilgun know each other as members of Rhodeo Poets, a group that meets at the library. They stressed that the evenings are designed to be inclusive and nonpartisan.
“This should be relaxing, welcoming,” Greene said. “No one should feel uncomfortable because they have a different outlook than we do. … It’s for entertainment. It’s for if you’ve got a talent that you’d like to show off for the first time, or you like performing, it’s supposed to be a little gift to the community, something that people can do and enjoy.”
The Ganny open-mic nights have proved to be so popular, they’ve even had a month with so many sign-ups that they had to add a second night.
“That says a lot about the talent in Jamestown and surrounding areas,” Gilgun said.
This came as no surprise to the organizers following the launch of the program in September.
“We had lots of sign-ups,” Gilgun said. “I couldn’t believe how many musicians were eager to perform and how good they were. We have a deep set of poets and other artists of the written word, and it was a success.”
“Wednesday Night Live” typically is from 7-9 p.m. with open slots for 20 performers, running the gamut from instrumentalists to spoken word. On any given night, they usually come close to filling all the slots, with at least 14 performers.
While there are regulars who can be expected to be on stage at every event, often newcomers will show up and register on the spot. Greene said her favorite thing is watching someone perform “who’s never put themselves out there.”
“It’s a perfect place to do it because it’s such a welcoming, supportive audience,” she said.
Performers are encouraged to sign up ahead of time by e-mailing wedsliveganny@gmail.com. The next open mic is Feb. 19.
“We get people from all over the place,” Greene said.
